newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to hold meetings on interstate meat issue.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to hold meetings on interstate meat issue.

text.p: The Agriculture Department said Friday it would hold two public meetings on the long-running issue of whether to permit interstate shipment of state-inspected meat and poultry products.
The department's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) said the meetings will be June 16 in Sioux Falls, S.D. and June 19 in Washington, D.C.
"FSIS is conducting these meetings to assist USDA in determining what additional steps are needed to resolve the interstate commerce issue," said agency chief Thomas Billy.
Currently, only federally-inspected meat and poultry products may be shipped across state lines.
Some state-inspected meat companies have been pressing the Agriculture Department to allow them to sell their products in other states without federal inspection.
Last month, the Ohio Department of Agriculture together with three Ohio meat packing companies and the Ohio Association of Meat Processors, sued the department to overturn the ban.

"USDA laws allows Canadian and Mexican meat to be sold all over the country, while meat inspected in Ohio by state inspectors can't even cross the state line into Indiana or Kentucky," said Ohio Attorney General Betty Montgomery, who filed the joint complaint.
The Ohioans argue that federal law already requires all state meat and poultry inspection programmes to be "at least equal to" federal standards.
U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman recently told a meeting of top state agriculture officials that he understood their concerns but did not want to risk public trust in food safety.

"Philosophically, I would like to see us move toward allowing state inspections but we're not there yet," the secretary said. He said new meat inspection rules requiring scientific testing for disease-causing bacteria needed to get into full swing.

The American Meat Institute, which represents meat packers, opposes the idea, saying the overwhelming majority of its members prefer one uniform federal inspection programme for products shipped across state lines or in international trade.
